product.title: Urdu 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Urdu: Nastaliq script with a pronunciation guide under every line of dialogue, word-for-word translations that show how Urdu builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a chart of all 39 letters, a close look at the ten letters Arabic doesn't have, the numbers 1–100, an A1 grammar summary, and the fifty most common verbs. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one point that most often trips learners up, from verbs that change with the speaker's gender to the little نے that turns the whole past-tense sentence around.

blocks.text: Urdu is closer to English than it looks. Behind the flowing script sits a distant cousin: Urdu and English both descend from the same Indo-European ancestor, which is why *nām* is "name", *do* is "two", and *tīn* is "three". Centuries of contact did the rest — English took *bazaar*, *pajamas*, *shampoo*, *jungle*, and *bungalow* from Urdu, and Urdu took *doctor*, *school*, *bus*, and *phone* from English. Two old roads meet in one language, and this course is built on both.

Urdu is spoken by around 230 million people. It's the national language of Pakistan, one of the official languages of India, and the everyday language of millions of migrants in the Gulf, the UK, and North America. If you've ever watched a Bollywood film and felt you nearly caught half a sentence, that's no accident: the language spoken on screen is, in its spoken form, the same language as Urdu.

This course uses what you already bring, but it doesn't pretend you're halfway there. The first real hurdle is the script: Urdu is written in an adapted Arabic alphabet of 39 letters, ten of which exist in neither Arabic nor Persian (ٹ ڈ ڑ ں ہ ھ ے پ چ گ). Without those ten you can't read a single Urdu sentence to the end. The pages ahead deal with all of them in one go.

One thing to make clear from the start: **reading Arabic letters is not the same as reading Urdu.** If you've learned to sound out Arabic — to read the Quran, say — that trained your eye to recognize shapes. Urdu asks for something else: recognizing shapes that **slope down diagonally** as they join (that's Nastaliq, the Urdu writing style), and then asking what the word means and why its ending changes when the speaker is a woman.

blocks.title: Three gifts and three traps
items: **Gift 1 — the alphabet is logical.** Twenty-nine of the thirty-nine Urdu letters are the Arabic letters, and once you learn the basic joining rules, every word is spelled the way it sounds — far more consistently than English.

**Gift 2 — you already own part of the vocabulary.** *Bazaar, pajamas, shampoo, jungle, bungalow, khaki, shawl, thug, loot, guru, pundit, cushy, verandah* went from Urdu into English; *doctor, school, hospital, station, ticket, phone* went the other way and are everyday Urdu.
**Gift 3 — no articles.** No *the*, no *a/an*. The word کتاب can mean "book", "a book", or "the book" — context does the work.

**Trap 1 — verbs know whether you're a man or a woman.** A man says میں جاتا ہوں and a woman says میں جاتی ہوں. Same sentence, different speaker. This starts in unit 2 and is practiced right up to the last unit.
**Trap 2 — prepositions come after.** "At home" is گھر میں, literally "home at". And the noun changes form when one attaches.
**Trap 3 — the نے that flips the past tense.** "I ate rice" becomes میں نے چاول کھایا, and the verb agrees with **the rice**, not with me. Unit 12 is devoted to it.

blocks.text: The twenty units ahead build on each other: each one reuses what the previous ones set up, and each targets exactly one point that most often trips up learners. Work through them in order, one unit per sitting, twenty to thirty minutes. By the end of unit 20 you'll be able to talk about yesterday, make plans for tomorrow, bargain at the bazaar, and write short messages that sound like someone from Lahore, not like a translation.

blocks.text: The pronunciation guide used in this course
A pronunciation guide in Latin letters is printed under every line of Urdu. It's there to help you in the first weeks, not to replace the script — from unit 10 on, try covering it with your finger.

blocks.title: Word stress isn't marked — and that's not an oversight
items: Unlike English, Urdu word stress **doesn't change meaning** and is never written. Give every syllable about the same weight, and lean a little on syllables with a **long vowel**. That's enough to sound natural.

What you really need to watch is **vowel length**. The word کم (*kam*, little) and the word کام (*kām*, work) differ only in that, and getting length wrong doesn't make your sentence sound wrong — it makes it **not sound like anything at all**, and your listener will ask you to repeat.
The Urdu full stop isn't "." but **۔** (khaṛī lakīr). The question mark **؟** and comma **،** face the opposite way from Latin ones. This course uses all three as they are.

blocks.text: One last piece of advice, and it matters most. Read the dialogues **aloud**. Urdu has sounds English doesn't — the retroflex ٹ ڈ ڑ and the aspirated کھ گھ — and those sounds can only be learned with your mouth, not your eyes. Five minutes of reading aloud a day beats an hour of silent reading.

front.title: Urdu words with a familiar ring

blocks.text: For centuries Persian was the language of the Mughal court, and through it Urdu absorbed a huge wave of Persian and Arabic words. The same wave reached Turkish, Swahili, and Malay — and some of it washed into English, often via British India. Here they are in one go: some will ring a bell at once, and the rest are worth learning as a set, because they share sounds (q, ḵ, ġ, z, f) and keep turning up.
Route one: through Persian and Arabic
Route two: through the family tree

This one is rarely noticed. The backbone of Urdu — its sentence structure, endings, and pronouns — isn't inherited from Arabic but from **ancient India**, the same family as Sanskrit. And Sanskrit is a distant cousin of English, Latin, and Greek. Some of the words below are true relatives of English words; others traveled into English during British rule.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Eight words that are easy to get wrong — especially if you know some Arabic
items: The word for woman is **عورت** *aurat*. In Arabic, *'awra* means the parts of the body to be covered; in Urdu, *aurat* is simply the most polite, ordinary word for "woman", used in the news and in law.
A house or building is **مکان** *makān* — in Arabic *makān* means "place". Don't confuse it with کھانا *khānā*, "to eat".
Face, appearance, or situation is **صورت** *sūrat* — not *sūra*, a chapter of the Quran. A letter you write and send is **خط** *ḵat*.
An office is **دفتر** *daftar* — in Arabic and Persian it's a notebook or register. A list is فہرست *fehrist*.
Poor is **غریب** *ġarīb* — in Arabic it means "strange". Strange in Urdu is عجیب *ajīb*.
An ordinary need is **ضرورت** *zarūrat*, not an emergency. "I need water" = مجھے پانی کی ضرورت ہے.
Price is **قیمت** *qīmat*. The similar-sounding قیامت means the Day of Judgment — a different word entirely.
Trouble or discomfort is **تکلیف** *taklīf*. A ready-made sentence: تکلیف کے لیے معذرت = "sorry for the trouble".

blocks.text: Don't memorize this page. Just know it's here, and come back whenever an Urdu word feels vaguely familiar — it usually is.

front.title: The Urdu script: 39 letters, ten of them unique

blocks.text: Urdu is written in the Arabic alphabet, reworked for the sounds of India. Twenty-nine of its letters are exactly the Arabic ones; the other ten were created specially and **exist in neither Arabic nor Persian**. If you already read Arabic, those ten are your homework for today; if you don't, start with them anyway — they're the letters that make Urdu look like Urdu.
Ten letters to learn first

Name

Example
Meaning

blocks.title: The letter ھ is the most important one on this page
items: The letter ھ (*do-chashmī he*, "two-eyed he") is never read on its own. It attaches after another letter and adds **one puff of breath**: the letter ک becomes کھ · the letter گ becomes گھ · the letter ت becomes تھ · the letter د becomes دھ · the letter پ becomes پھ · the letter ب becomes بھ · the letter چ becomes چھ · the letter ٹ becomes ٹھ · the letter ڈ becomes ڈھ · and the letter ڑ becomes ڑھ.

The difference changes meaning, and English speakers tend to blur it: **پل** *pal* (bridge) versus **پھل** *phal* (fruit). **کان** *kān* (ear) versus **کھان** *khān*. **بال** *bāl* (hair) versus **بھال**. English does have both sounds — the *p* in *pin* is aspirated, the *p* in *spin* isn't — but it never uses them to tell words apart.

How to practice: hold your palm ten centimeters in front of your mouth. Say *pal* like the *p* in *spin* — your palm feels nothing. Say *phal* — your palm should feel a puff of air. If you don't feel it, the aspiration isn't there yet.

blocks.text: Twenty-nine letters shared with Arabic

blocks.title: Good news about ث ذ ص ض ط ظ
items: These six letters are still written because the words come from Arabic, but in Urdu **their sounds have merged**. The letters ث ص س are all read **s**. The letters ذ ز ض ظ are all read **z**. The letters ت and ط are both **t**.
In other words, you don't need to practice a single new sound for these six letters — you just learn each word's spelling, exactly as you learn that *phone* is spelled with ph and not f.
On the other hand, one sound that English lacks is **fully alive** in Urdu: ق is pronounced far back in the throat (قیمت *qīmat*, price) and shouldn't turn into a k.

blocks.text: The joining rules are the same as in Arabic: ا د ذ ر ز ژ و never join to the following letter, and all the others do. What's **different** is the style. Urdu is written in **Nastaliq**, which slopes down each word diagonally from top right to bottom left, instead of running flat like the Naskh style used for Arabic. This whole course is printed in Nastaliq, so your eyes get used to the forms you'll actually meet in Pakistan.
These pages aren't for studying but for quick reference. Everything here is explained step by step in the units; unit numbers are given so you can go back to the full explanation.
Personal pronouns and "to be" (units 1, 16)
The possessive کا / کے / کی (unit 4)

It agrees with **the thing owned**, not the owner. علی کا بیٹا (Ali's son) · علی کی بیٹی (Ali's daughter) · علی کے بیٹے (Ali's sons). Special forms for pronouns: میرا/میری/میرے · تمہارا · آپ کا · اس کا · ہمارا.
Postpositions and the oblique form (unit 6)

blocks.text: ⚠️ Masculine nouns ending in ـا change to ـے before a postposition, so لڑکا is used as لڑکے کو. The plural changes to ـوں, so لڑکے is used as لڑکوں کو. Feminine nouns don't change in the singular, but their plural also becomes ـوں, so لڑکیاں is used as لڑکیوں کو.

blocks.text: Word order (units 1, 6)

**Subject — adverbs — object — verb.** The verb almost always comes last, with "to be" right after it. The sentence میں کل لاہور جاؤں گا = "I tomorrow Lahore will-go". Yes/no questions: put کیا at the **very front**. Wh-questions: the question word goes right before the verb.
Dative sentences — the experiencer takes کو (units 10, 15, 18)

head: Formula
Example
Literally
rows: to-me tea pleasing is — *I like tea*
to-me head pain is — *I have a headache*

blocks.text: The short forms of کو are مجھے (to me) · تمہیں (to you, familiar) · آپ کو (to you, polite) · اسے (to him/her) · ہمیں (to us) · انہیں (to them).
Negation (units 9, 12, 16)

The ordinary negative is **نہیں**, and it goes **right before the verb**: میں نہیں جاتا. In habitual sentences ہوں/ہے/ہیں is usually **dropped**: میں نہیں جاتا, not میں نہیں جاتا ہوں. To tell someone not to do something, use **مت**: مت جاؤ. And **نہ** is used in the subjunctive and in compound sentences.

back.title: Numbers 1–100 and how to use them

blocks.text: This is the part of Urdu that takes the most memorizing, and it's best to know that from the start so you don't blame yourself. Unlike English, which builds "twenty-three" from "twenty" and "three", Urdu has **a hundred words that each stand on their own**. The word تیئس (23) can't be guessed from تین (3) and بیس (20) — it has to be learned.

The good news: the patterns are still there. Almost every number ends in the sound of its tens (ـیس for the 20s, ـتیس for the 30s, ـالیس for the 40s, ـاون for the 50s) and begins with a worn-down form of its units. After two weeks, your ear guesses far better than your eye.

blocks.title: Big numbers — and two words with no English equivalent
items: A hundred is سو *sau* · a thousand ہزار *hazār* · a hundred thousand **لاکھ** *lākh* · ten million **کروڑ** *karoṛ*.

Those two units — لاکھ and کروڑ — have no one-word equivalent in English, and the whole Urdu-speaking world counts with them. House prices, national budgets, and audience figures are all given in لاکھ and کروڑ, not in millions. Two million rupees = بیس لاکھ روپے, literally "twenty lakh".

Fractions to learn because they're used every day: half **آدھا** *ādhā* · one and a half **ڈیڑھ** *ḍeṛh* · two and a half **ڈھائی** *ḍhāī* · three and a half **ساڑھے تین** *sāṛhe tīn*. From 3½ up the pattern is regular: ساڑھے + number.

Urdu numbers can be written with Eastern digits ۰۱۲۳۴۵۶۷۸۹ — note that ۴ ۵ ۶ have the Persian shapes and **differ from Arabic ٤ ٥ ٦**. In everyday Pakistan the Latin digits 0–9 are common too; this course uses Latin digits to keep the load light.

blocks.text: Every Urdu verb ends in ـنا in its dictionary form. Drop ـنا, and what's left is the **stem**, used for every form: the stem of کرنا is کر, and the stem of جانا is جا. The last column gives the past form, because that's where all the irregularities live.

blocks.title: Six irregular past forms — just learn them
items: Only these six: the past of کرنا is کیا, not کرا · the past of جانا is گیا · the past of لینا is لیا · the past of دینا is دیا · the past of پینا is پیا · and the past of ہونا is ہوا.

That's it. Six words. Every other Urdu verb forms its past by adding ـا / ـی / ـے to the stem with no surprises. Compared with English and its hundreds of irregular verbs, that's a very short list — and one reason Urdu is much easier than it looks.

⚠️ Remember unit 12: once the verb is **transitive** and the sentence is **past**, the subject takes نے and the verb agrees with the **object**. For example میں نے چائے پی, with the form پی because چائے is feminine. Four verbs in this list look transitive but **never take** نے at all — لانا، بھولنا، ملنا، بولنا.

blocks.text: If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you have something real: about 600 words, the whole framework of basic verbs, and the ability to make up your own sentences about today, yesterday, and tomorrow. That's genuine A1 — not a list of memorized phrases, but a small engine you can run yourself.
Three things that help most now

items: **Watch Bollywood with English subtitles.** The spoken language of Indian films is the same Urdu-Hindi. Start with family films with slow dialogue, and count how many words you catch every ten minutes. That number rises much faster than you'd expect.

**Read the headlines, not the articles.** Sites like BBC اردو and Dawn's Urdu edition publish dozens of short headlines every day. Headlines are the densest, most repetitive Urdu text there is — ten a day for a month will teach you to read Nastaliq fast.

**Write three sentences a day.** About anything: what you ate, where you went, what you'll do tomorrow. Three sentences, in a notes app, with an Urdu keyboard. Writing forces you to choose جاتا or جاتی, and that choice is what makes the grammar stick.

blocks.text: Where to go after A1

Urdu A2 centers on three things deliberately left out of this course: **compound verbs** (کھا لینا، کر دینا، بول اٹھنا — verb pairs that shift the nuance, the heart of conversational Urdu), **linked sentences with کہ and جو**, and **indirect polite forms** used at work and in formal letters. All three are much easier to set up once the A1 framework is solid — and that framework is now in place.

blocks.title: If you'd like to continue with a teacher
items: Private Urdu lessons at Linguo are one-on-one over Zoom, scheduled around your time, and your teacher adapts the material to your goals — working in the Gulf, reading poetry, or simply talking with your extended family.
This course can be used as class material: bring the unit you're working on, and spend class time speaking, not rereading.
Find out more at **linguo.id**.
